summary.text: 西 is the character for “west.” One disputed interpretation sees its whole graph as a bird’s nest. Reusing that sign for “west” because the words sounded alike is a hypothesis: the nest’s name and pronunciation are unknown, so the sound match cannot be demonstrated. A separate explanation links west with sunset and birds roosting.

formation.text: A traditional pictographic analysis treats the whole graph as a bird’s nest, without dividing it into modern-looking parts. One proposed route to “west” is that the nest sign was reused for a similar-sounding word, but the nest’s name and pronunciation are not established, so this sound match remains unproven. A competing explanation connects west with birds roosting at sunset. Another proposal links a different early form with 囟 through sound similarity; these analyses remain unsettled.

components.text: One disputed pictorial interpretation reads the whole graph as a bird’s nest. This does not establish the object’s name or prove how the graph came to mean “west.”

history.text: Graphic records identify oracle-bone, bronze, Chu manuscript, and small-seal stages, but do not establish a detailed sequence of stroke changes. The curated seal-script image is a modern vector reconstruction, not a dated artifact, and does not resolve the origin dispute.
A separate proposal holds that one early form borrowed 囟 because the ancient words sounded similar, and that this form later developed into 西. This proposed graphic history remains unsettled.

uncertainties.text: The nest interpretation, the proposal involving 囟, and the bag-or-basket account are competing explanations; the evidence here does not settle the origin. For the nest account, it is unresolved whether “west” was written by sound-based reuse of the sign or arose through the sunset association.
No supported name or pronunciation for a depicted nest, bag, or basket is available to establish a sound match with the directional word.

limitations.text: The accounts do not establish whether the western-direction use arose by reusing the graph for a similar-sounding word or through a semantic association with sunset and roosting. No individually dated examples establish the sequence.
